We celebrated Easter at a tiny village church in the Peloponnese last year: midnight service, every candle lit from a single flame, and the whole congregation walking out into the dark singing. Afterwards, fireworks and lamb on spits in the square. Grandmothers kissed me on both cheeks. I'm not Orthodox, but I came home moved in a way that Sunday mornings usually don't manage. Christos Anesti.

Ramadan this year was a mix of hard and beautiful. Long days, short nights, cousins arriving at the door with dates at sunset, my grandfather leading the prayer, my teenage nephew fasting for the first time and refusing to admit he was starving. We broke the fast with soup on the balcony, the whole street smelling of cooking. I'll miss it for the next eleven months. Ramadan Kareem, everyone. 🌙

The book of Job has no easy answers, and that's why I love it. His friends offer neat theology, and by the end God rebukes them, not Job. Job's grief is allowed to be loud. Job's questions are allowed to be angry. We don't need to tidy suffering into a lesson. Sometimes the faithful response is to sit in silence for seven days and listen, as his friends did before they started talking.

Genesis 1 and 2 give two different accounts of creation, with different order and different emphasis. Rather than a contradiction, many scholars think they come from distinct traditions woven together by an editor who didn't want to lose either. It's a way of reading that makes the text richer, not weaker. If you want a good starting point, try Robert Alter's translation and commentary.

Our Diwali party had 30 people, 4 cuisines, and one incident involving a sparkler and the neighbour's hedge. Nobody was hurt. The hedge forgave us. We lit diyas on every windowsill, made rangoli in the hallway, and danced until the downstairs neighbours came up to join. This is what a festival of lights should be, a very loud, very warm evening shared with people you love. Happy Diwali! 🪔✨

Reading Psalms in the middle of the night as a new mum. Psalm 63: "On my bed I remember you, I think of you through the watches of the night." It's a strange, tender line for those of us up at 3am with a screaming baby. It's become a quiet little mantra. If you're awake with someone small tonight, you're not alone. #bible #newmum

Honestly, what a weekend of football. Arsenal beat Spurs in the north London derby with a 93rd-minute header, Real Madrid came from two goals down in the Champions League, and the Premier League table is now so tight that three teams are separated by a single point. My throat is raw and my voice is gone. I've watched four matches in two days and my wife has asked me to "please go outside". Worth every second. #COYG

My local club, the Heat? No, not that one, it's a village side in the fourth tier, and we just lost 6-0 to our biggest rivals in front of 112 people. But the bar after the match was packed, the manager bought a round, the goalkeeper (who let in all six) got a standing ovation for his bravery, and we're hosting the rematch in March. This is why I love grassroots sport. It's about the people, not the table.

If you've never been to a baseball game in person, go. I don't care which team. The Yankees game I went to last weekend had a rain delay, a bad hot dog, a five-year-old yelling at the umpire, and a walk-off home run in the 11th that made the whole stadium shake. A kid next to me cried. His dad cried. I cried. I know nothing about the infield fly rule and I had the time of my life. ⚾

The Lakers' new coach is trying to reinvent their offence and so far it looks like a group of strangers trying to share a taxi. There's talent, but no rhythm. I give it until February. If the trade deadline passes and nobody has been moved, I'm cancelling my season ticket. Ok I'm not. I'll never cancel. I'm in too deep after 27 years. #LakeShow

Went to my first live Premier League match last weekend, a drab 0-0, and it was brilliant. The songs, the pies, the guy behind me who analysed every pass like a university lecturer. Nothing happened and somehow everything happened. My son, who's eight, fell asleep in the second half and woke up for the final whistle. He asked if we could come back. Yes, mate. Every year.

The Olympics are meant to bring people together, but the legacy question always comes back to money. London 2012 left a park and a stadium that's still in use. Athens 2004 left abandoned venues. Rio 2016 left debts. If LA 2028 can reuse existing arenas, as promised, it might actually be the first sensible Olympics in decades. I'd love to be proven wrong. https://example.com/olympics

Ali's fights are still taught in boxing gyms, but what I love most is his interviews. He was a master of language, the original trash-talker, and he was quicker with a rhyme than any rapper I know. The Rumble in the Jungle in 1974 was as much a psychological battle as a physical one. He let George Foreman punch himself out against the ropes. Rope-a-dope. Pure genius.

Spent 3 hours debugging why a deploy kept failing and the cause was a trailing space in an environment variable. A trailing space. I want to put a plaque on my desk that says "check the whitespace first." Developers, share your most embarrassing root cause so I feel better. Mine's a missing comma in a JSON file that took down staging for an hour. #devlife #debugging

Not a hot take, just a fact: no one reads the terms and conditions, including the people who wrote them. I recently compared three popular apps and the privacy policies add up to roughly 38,000 words. At a normal reading speed, that's over three hours for three apps. You can't consent to something you can't read. We need shorter, plainer, standardised summaries. https://example.com/privacy

My team just moved from Windows 10 to Windows 11 and, honestly, the transition was smoother than I expected. A few driver hiccups, a printer that refused to cooperate, and a Start menu that moved to the centre. Nothing dramatic. Our IT lead gave a 20-minute training and people adapted in a day. Boring successes are the best kind. 🙌

There's an interesting security story from Apple this week: a researcher found a flaw in the way the iPhone handles messaging attachments, reported it responsibly, and the company shipped a patch in under 10 days. That's the way the system should work. Update your phone. It takes five minutes and could save you a lot of grief.

Tesla's factory in Texas is a wild place. I toured it last month, and the scale of it is hard to imagine: a building the size of several football pitches, robots moving in perfect rhythm, and a long conveyor of finished cars. Everything's loud and clean at the same time. Whatever you think about the company, the manufacturing is impressive. #Tesla

The Uber Eats app showed me a restaurant that closed in 2022, a courier who was 40 minutes away, and a promo code that expired yesterday. At some point we need to ask whether the app experience matches the marketing. Small bugs add up. I'm switching back to ordering directly from the local places, and tipping in cash. https://example.com/rant

I used the word "Avatar" in a meeting today to describe a profile picture, and a colleague asked if I meant the one with the blue people. No, Janet. The little round image at the top of your chat window. That's an avatar. It's also what we call the character you control in a virtual world. The word has been around since Sanskrit, long before pixels.

Spent Sunday making stock from scratch: roasted chicken carcass, carrots, onion, bay leaf, peppercorns, a splash of vinegar, six hours on a low simmer. The apartment smelled like a restaurant kitchen. Strained it, cooled it, froze it in 500ml tubs. By Wednesday I'd made risotto, a soup and a stew from it. A rainy weekend, a big pot, and a freezer full of liquid gold. Highly recommend. 🍲

Went to a tasting menu at a fancy Paris restaurant for my wife's birthday. Eleven courses, three hours, a bill that made me dizzy. The standout was a single scallop in a broth so clear and clean that we both went silent. The dessert was a chocolate sphere that you crack with a spoon. Was it worth the money? Once, yes. Would I do it twice? Honestly, no. I'd rather eat tacos on a street corner.

My Dubai friends insist I try camel-milk ice cream, so I did, at a market in Al Quoz. It was surprisingly good, a bit salty, a bit tangy, with a hint of caramel. I'm still thinking about the pistachio topping. If you're ever in the UAE and see it, order the small cup first. Then order a second. #foodie

The local butcher gave me advice on how to cook a lamb shoulder: low and slow, 150°C, five hours, wrapped in foil with garlic, rosemary, and a good splash of white wine. It fell apart with a spoon. My dinner guests asked for the recipe, which I'm putting here for the world. Shout-out to Dave at the shop for the tip. Support your local butcher, he knows more than any recipe site.

There's a Lagos buka near my office that serves amala and ewedu for the equivalent of about two dollars, and the line is out the door by 12:30. The woman running it, Mama Tosin, recognises everyone and shouts orders in rapid-fire Yoruba. It's the best lunch in the city and she's never advertised once. If you're ever in Ikeja, find it. Bring cash.

The Easter bread in my family is a braided loaf with a hard-boiled egg baked into the middle, glazed with honey and sprinkled with sesame seeds. My grandmother's recipe, my mother's hands, and now mine. We make six every year, one for each household. Making it together is the whole point. By the time it comes out of the oven, the kitchen is warm, loud and perfect.

Tried making sushi at home for the first time, and my verdict: it's harder than it looks and still worth it. The rice is the whole game. Wash it, soak it, cook it, season it with vinegar while warm, and don't squish it. My rolls looked like they'd been hit by a bus, but they tasted great. Next time I'll try a bamboo mat. Please send me any tips. 🍣

Spent a week driving the Pacific Coast Highway, San Francisco to LA, in a small rented hatchback. Foggy mornings in Big Sur, sunsets at Morro Bay, elephant seals at San Simeon, and a roadside diner in a town I've forgotten the name of where the pie was legendary. No schedule, no plan, just a playlist and a map. If you've got ten days and a licence, do it.

My top tips for visiting Paris on a budget: stay outside the centre, buy a weekly metro pass, picnic in the park instead of eating out at every meal, skip the Eiffel Tower summit and go to the viewpoint at Montparnasse instead, and spend your money on the one thing you'll never forget. For us it was a seat at a tiny jazz club in Saint-Germain. €15 and magical.

Taking my family to Alaska in July. Four days in Anchorage, three in Denali, one on a glacier cruise. We've booked a camper trailer for the middle section and I'm terrified of the mosquitos. Please send tips on bug spray, bear spray and anything else that starts with "spray". Also suggestions for the best fish and chips in Seward. #Alaska

A weekend in Vegas without gambling is possible. We saw a show, hiked at Red Rock Canyon, ate at every buffet, drove to the Hoover Dam, and had a sunrise breakfast in the desert. We spent about $400 each. The city is a lot more than slot machines if you let it be. The hotel pool alone is worth the trip in July.

Visiting Lincoln in England last weekend: the cathedral dominates the whole skyline, the hill climb from the old town is brutal, and the pubs at the top are very good. Steep Hill is not a joke. I went up three times and complained all three. Gorgeous medieval streets, friendly people, and the best sausage rolls I've had in years.

Our flight to Rome got delayed by eight hours, so we spent the evening in the airport playing cards and eating overpriced pasta. A group of retired Texans adopted us and by midnight we were all singing. We landed at 3am and slept through the first day. Next time I'll book the morning flight. But honestly, I'd do the whole delay again for the company.

It's the little things I've started appreciating at 35: a quiet morning, a clean kitchen, a good pen, a bed that's made, a message from an old friend. None of it costs much, and all of it matters. I used to chase big wins, and now I chase small calm. It's less impressive on Instagram and much better for my blood pressure. #gratitude

Someone at my gym asked how I stay consistent and I said honestly: I don't. I stay inconsistent, but I return. A missed week isn't a failed month, and a bad day isn't a bad year. Return, return, return. That's the secret, if there is one. Be gentle on yourself and show up again on Tuesday.

Just finished sorting through my late father's bookshelf. Hundreds of paperbacks, a few signed first editions, notes in the margins, a pressed flower between two pages of a poetry anthology. I had to stop several times. We're keeping about 40 and donating the rest to the library. It took four weekends. I'm glad I did it slowly. Every book had a little of him in it. 📚

A year ago I could barely leave my flat without a panic attack. Last week I sat in a crowded café for an hour, read a book, drank a flat white, and walked home the long way. That might sound small to you but it was the biggest day of my year. If you're in the hard bit, hold on. It does shift. Slowly, then suddenly.

Wondering whether anyone else struggles with the "Sunday scaries." Around 4pm every Sunday my brain starts replaying everything that could go wrong next week. I've tried exercise, journaling, tea, and a gratitude list. What works for me now is cooking a big meal and prepping lunches. Having a plan quiets the noise. Curious what works for you.

I spent my 30th birthday alone in a tiny cottage in Cornwall, no phone, no plans, just long walks and a stack of paperbacks. It was the best present I've ever given myself. People kept asking if I was lonely, and I realised that solitude and loneliness are different things. One is a place you visit, the other a place you're stuck.

My 2024 in numbers: 3 jobs applied for, 1 job landed, 7 books started, 4 finished, 150 runs, 2 grandparents lost, 1 niece born, 12 haircuts, and about 30 voicemails I never returned. It was a hard, strange, in-between kind of year. But it ends with a lot of love around me. On to the next. #YearInReview

The siege of Constantinople in 1453 was a turning point for three reasons: the use of giant cannons, the collapse of Byzantine defences, and the sheer scale of the Ottoman army. Mehmed II was 21 years old. The city fell after 53 days. Some historians say it marks the end of the Middle Ages, though that's too tidy. It did, however, reorder the trade routes and push Europeans to look for new ways to the East.

Napoleon's Russian campaign of 1812 is usually blamed on the winter, but most of his army was already gone by autumn. Disease, desertion and starvation killed hundreds of thousands before the first big snow. Out of roughly 600,000 men who crossed the Niemen, fewer than 100,000 came back. The cold was the last act, not the cause. Logistics, as always, was the real enemy.

Cleopatra's Alexandria was one of the great cities of the ancient world, with a lighthouse that stood for more than a thousand years, a library that attracted scholars from every corner of the Mediterranean, and a palace district that now lies under the sea. Divers have found sphinxes, columns and statues in the harbour. Whatever the legends say, the real city was more astonishing.

Titanic is often remembered for the iceberg, but the sinking raised hard questions about class, regulation and communication. Wireless operators got ice warnings from other ships that never reached the bridge. Nearby vessels didn't respond to flares. And the lifeboat regulations were set for ships that were half the size. The British inquiry led to the first international Safety of Life at Sea convention in 1914. Disaster, then reform.

People like to quote the Lincoln-Douglas debates of 1858 as a golden age of public argument, and in some ways they were: seven debates, three hours each, tens of thousands of listeners standing in the open air. But the speeches were also full of racial language that we'd find shocking now. Both things are true. History is best read with complexity and not as a morality play.

I recently visited the Apollo mission control room in Houston, which has been restored to how it looked in 1969. The consoles, the ashtrays, the tiny screens, the cheap plastic cups. It's astounding to think the world's greatest technological feat was done in a room with less computing power than a modern toaster. And the people were mostly in their 20s. Remarkable.

Gandhi's 1930 salt march took 24 days and covered about 390 km. He started with 78 followers, and by the time he got to Dandi thousands had joined. The act of picking up a lump of natural salt was a deliberate breach of the colonial salt tax. Newspapers worldwide covered it. It showed how a small, symbolic act of civil disobedience can reshape a political argument.

The Chernobyl 1986 accident released about 400 times more radioactive material than the Hiroshima bomb, according to the IAEA. But radiation exposure varied widely. People in the 30 km exclusion zone had much larger doses than those in other parts of Europe. About 30 plant workers and firefighters died within weeks. Long-term cancer estimates range from a few thousand to tens of thousands, depending on the model. The honest answer is that we're still learning.

The physics of gravity is deceptively strange. Newton described it as a force that acts at a distance. Einstein replaced that with a curve in spacetime. Quantum theory wants it to be a particle called a graviton, but nobody has found one. We can predict the orbit of a spacecraft to the metre, and yet we can't reconcile the best theories of the very small and the very large. Wonderful, annoying, unsolved.

Oppenheimer's 1939 paper on neutron stars, written with Volkoff, was the first to calculate the limit above which a star would collapse. Today it's called the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit. It's a cornerstone of how we understand black holes. His other work on quantum mechanics matters too. The man did a lot more than lead a lab at Los Alamos, and physicists know it. #physics

There's a persistent myth that we only use 10% of our brains. It isn't true. Brain scans show activity throughout the brain, even during sleep. Damage to almost any area has some consequence. The myth probably started with a misquote of William James, who said that people don't reach their full potential. If you want to stay sharp, sleep and exercise matter more than any gadget.

If you visit the Apollo exhibit at the Smithsonian, don't miss the little case with the actual flight checklists, the spiral-bound ones with coffee stains. They're a reminder that missions to the Moon were run by humans with pencils and procedures. Every item had a backup, every backup had a backup, and every astronaut had practised the whole thing hundreds of times. Reliability is a team sport.

Tesla's early AC experiments at the Chicago World's Fair in 1893 lit up more than 90,000 lamps and persuaded sceptics that alternating current was practical. Edison's camp fought hard, including a sinister public campaign to scare people about AC. In the end physics won over marketing. It's one of the great stories in the history of engineering, and I'd love to see more of it taught in schools.

The brain doesn't distinguish well between real and imagined practice, according to a study of pianists. One group practised a five-finger exercise for two hours a day; another group only imagined doing it. After five days, both groups showed similar changes in motor cortex activity. Visualisation isn't a replacement for practice, but it's a legitimate supplement. Weird and wonderful. #neuroscience

My first Taylor Swift concert, last night in Vegas. I'm a 42-year-old man who went along because my daughter couldn't find another chaperone. I came out singing every word, wearing a friendship bracelet that a 12-year-old gave me, and apparently crying during "All Too Well". The whole stadium sang as one. I don't care about the discourse. It was a night I'll never forget. 🎤

I fell into a Dylan rabbit hole this weekend and discovered how many versions of "Blowin' in the Wind" exist: the original from 1963, a gospel arrangement, a live version from the Concert for Bangladesh, a surprisingly good reggae cover, and one by a school choir in Dublin. A song that simple and that open is basically a folk tradition now. It belongs to everyone. #BobDylan

The Lennon memorial in Central Park, Strawberry Fields, was packed on a grey Sunday. A busker was playing "Imagine" on an out-of-tune guitar and everybody was singing along. Strangers, locals, kids on scooters, a man in a tuxedo. Nobody cared that the guitar was flat. It's a place for people who still want that song to be true. John would've smiled. 🕊️

If you only know "Hound Dog" and "Jailhouse Rock," go listen to Elvis's gospel albums. His rendition of "How Great Thou Art" is one of the finest vocal performances of the 20th century, and he's clearly not performing for the cameras. Just a man singing something he believes. It's from 1967 and still gives me goosebumps every time. #Elvis

Local music scene in Brooklyn this week: a free jazz night at a bookshop in Fort Greene, a kids' bluegrass session in Prospect Park, a punk gig in a converted garage in Bushwick, and an open-mic at a bar that's been running since 1987. This city never stops. If you're bored, you're not looking. #BrooklynMusic

Just rewatched... no wait, relistened. The 1971 live recording of Aretha Franklin at the Fillmore West is one of the best albums of all time. Ray Charles introduces her, the band is on fire, and Aretha takes the hippie crowd and sends them to church. She sings "Respect" like she's reclaiming the world. 52 years on and the energy hasn't dimmed. Play it loud.

Hot take: every playlist should end on a slow song. People spend hours curating the first 30 minutes and then let the last track be random. A good last song is like a last line in a book. It's what you carry with you into the next hour. Mine for the evening: Nina Simone, "Here Comes the Sun". Whatever you pick, make it count.

Our village was cut off for two days by the snow. Roads closed, power out, the pub generator keeping the whole community fed. Neighbours knocked on doors to check on the elderly, a farmer dragged people's cars out with his tractor, and the vicar organised soup and sandwiches in the church hall. It was a bit of a nightmare and also, weirdly, the best I've felt about the place in years.

It hit 47°C in the Sahara last week while Siberia was in the middle of a heatwave too. I can't be the only one who looks at global weather maps and thinks something has gone sideways. Climate variation is natural, but this is a bigger pattern, and the data, from NASA, NOAA, the Met Office, all point in the same direction. Check the numbers, not the headlines.

Hurricane warning for the Florida Keys, evacuations underway. My cousin in Key West sent a photo of her empty fridge, a bag by the door, and her cat in a carrier. She's heading north with a convoy of neighbours. Everyone's hoping the storm veers. I'd say a prayer, but honestly I'm just refreshing the weather channel every two minutes. Be safe out there. #Hurricane

The Dubai rain last year shut down the whole city for two days. Streets flooded, malls leaked, airport runways under water. Everyone was laughing at first, because it almost never rains, but the drainage wasn't designed for it. Engineers are now re-doing the stormwater system, which will cost billions. It's a good reminder that infrastructure is built for the weather it expects, not the weather it gets.

Pro tip for anyone camping in the rain: pitch on a slight slope, dig a drainage trench, put a tarp over the top, store dry clothes in a sealed bag, and keep a spare lighter in your sock. We did four days in the Lake District in constant rain last week and had a brilliant time. The sheep were not impressed. Neither was the dog. #camping

Anyone else watching the aurora forecast tonight? NOAA says it's a G4 geomagnetic storm, and people as far south as Alabama might see it. I'm in Texas and I've never seen one. I'm sitting in a field 30 miles outside the city with a thermos, a camping chair, and a very patient friend. If I see a green streak I'll cry. Updates to follow.

I love autumn rain. The smell of wet leaves, the golden light between showers, the sound on the window while I read. People complain, and yes, getting soaked on the commute isn't fun, but a rainy Sunday with a blanket and a pot of tea is one of life's great pleasures. Season of mellow fruitfulness and all that. 🍂

Our company just had its annual review season and, as ever, the process was a series of forms, feedback, calibration meetings and one very awkward chat with my director about "growth opportunities". The real feedback came during a coffee break with a colleague who said, "You're good at the thing nobody else wants to do." Fair. It's what I'm known for, apparently. Looking for a bigger challenge in 2025.

Interviewing hundreds of candidates for a software role taught me a few things: nobody reads the job description, the best people often have the shortest CVs, and a single warm email beats ten cold ones. Also, please don't lie about your skills. A senior engineer asked one question about the thing you listed and the whole interview unravelled. Honesty works. #hiring

I want to talk about the "quiet quitting" debate and why it makes me tired. Doing the job you're paid for, and then going home, isn't quitting. It's a job. If your employer expects unpaid weekends, call it what it is. I've been in plenty of workplaces that praised overwork and then laid people off with an email. Loyalty goes both ways or it doesn't go at all.

Three years ago I joined a tiny company with 8 people. Today we're 85. The big change isn't the office, the budget or the clients. It's the meetings. We used to decide things in a corridor in two minutes. Now it takes an agenda, a pre-read and three follow-ups. I'm not against growth, but I do miss the corridor. If anyone has solved this, tell me how.

A word for anyone starting a new job this week: ask questions, take notes, find the person who has been there longest and buy them a coffee. Nobody expects you to know everything on day one. Nobody remembers your first-week mistakes after month two. Don't compare your chapter one to someone else's chapter fifteen. You'll be fine.

Why does every office have one person who microwaves salmon at 12:15? One. Always one. We have a policy now. It's in the shared drive. It's called "the fish rule". The person is still unrepentant. HR has had two meetings about it. Our director says it's "a culture matter". This is what we pay a mortgage for.

A tip from fifteen years of running meetings: the first five minutes decide everything. Start on time. State the purpose. Name the decision you need. Assign a note-taker. And end five minutes early so people can breathe. Nobody has ever complained that a meeting finished early. Apply it for a week and see how your team reacts.

Wall Street's wobble this week has everybody posting charts, and I just want to remind everyone that markets go up and down, and that a one-week move isn't a trend. I check my portfolio once a month. I rebalance once a year. I invest regularly regardless of headlines. It's not clever, it's boring, and so far it works. Not financial advice, just a person who sleeps well. #investing

We just finished our annual financial review as a family and found that the biggest single leak was subscriptions: streaming, apps, a gym membership nobody used, a magazine we forgot about. Total £94 a month. We cancelled all but three. That alone pays for a family weekend break each quarter. Do an audit. Open your bank statement. You'll find a surprise or two.

A friend asked whether to buy a Tesla or a used Honda. I asked what the car's for. Commuting 12 miles? Honda. Road trips with chargers on the route? Tesla might be great. Total cost of ownership matters more than sticker price: insurance, depreciation, repairs, and charging. Run the spreadsheet. If your cheaper option has a cost per mile that's half, that tells you something.

Just filed taxes and it took three hours, two cups of coffee, and one panic over a form I couldn't find. Pro tip: keep a folder, digital or paper, where every tax-related doc goes the moment it arrives. January me thanked December me. Next year I'm starting in February. #TaxSeason

Money lessons I wish someone had taught me at 20: automate your savings, don't carry a credit card balance, keep your fixed costs low, spend on experiences that you'll remember, and talk about money with friends and partners. The taboo makes it harder. Also: learn what compound interest does. Nothing else comes close, and the earlier you start, the more it does.

Hear me out: the "latte factor" argument is mostly nonsense. Skipping coffee won't make you rich. The things that matter are housing, transport and food at home, and earning more. Of course small leaks add up, but if you're drowning in rent, a flat white isn't the culprit. Stop blaming individuals for a structural problem. Rant over.

Mental health tip that sounds boring and works: a 20-minute walk without headphones. No podcast, no music, just you and the street. At first it feels weird and uncomfortable, then your brain starts to wander in a good way. I've solved more problems on these walks than at my desk. If you're stuck, step outside. It's free. #wellbeing

Three months into learning to manage my type 2 diabetes. Cut sugar, started a daily walk, and began eating more vegetables and lentils. My blood sugar is in range for the first time in two years, and I've lost 9kg. It wasn't a miracle, it was boring, steady habits. If your doctor says "lifestyle", ask for specifics and a plan, and keep a log.

Breaking my silence about my cancer scare in the hope it helps someone. I found a lump in January and delayed going to the doctor for six weeks because I was scared. When I finally went, the scan, biopsy and results took ten days. It was benign. I could have saved myself six weeks of terror by going immediately. If something doesn't feel right, don't wait. Book it today.

It took me years to understand that rest isn't the opposite of productivity, it's part of it. When I sleep well, I'm sharper, kinder and funnier. When I skip sleep, I'm none of those. Everyone says "I'll sleep when I'm dead", but you'll be a lot less fun in the meantime. Protect your sleep like you protect your phone battery. #selfcare

Our local hospital has opened a new walk-in clinic and I want to say thank you. Went in with a broken wrist on Saturday night, was seen in 20 minutes, X-rayed in 40, and had a cast on by 11pm. The nurse made a joke about my handwriting on the form and the doctor drew a smiley face on my cast. That's the human side of medicine.

Learning about my own heart this week. I had palpitations, and the cardiologist put me on a 24-hour monitor. The verdict: harmless extra beats, triggered by too much caffeine and too little sleep. A small lifestyle change and I'm fine. It's remarkable how much you learn from a short test and a patient doctor. Get checked if your heart worries you.

Went to a free flu clinic at the library and was in and out in 7 minutes. The volunteer pharmacist chatted to everyone in the queue. We had biscuits. I got a sticker. I realise that for some people this is a normal Tuesday, but for me it was a cheerful reminder that public health can feel like community. Get your jab, folks. #FluSeason

I wrote my daughter a letter for her 18th birthday, to be opened in ten years. I told her what her seven-year-old self was like: the lisp, the endless questions, how she held my hand on the way to school. I told her I was proud and that I wasn't perfect. I put it in a time capsule with a photo and a pressed flower. I can't wait for her to read it.

Our family has a rule: at dinner everyone shares their "high, low and buffalo" of the day, a high point, a low point, and something random. The buffalo is usually the funniest. Last night it was my son's account of a squirrel in the school hall. My husband's buffalo was a spider. I love this ritual because it brings everything out in the open without anyone feeling interrogated.

My grandmother taught me how to knit when I was nine, and I'm 41 now, sitting on the sofa with a half-finished scarf. She passed away last spring. Every time I drop a stitch I can hear her saying "slowly, love, slowly". The scarf won't be perfect. It's going to be a bit too wide and a bit wonky. I'm going to wear it all winter and think of her. 🧶

It's a strange feeling to take your elderly dad to a hospital appointment and notice how much he's slowed down. The man who taught me to ride a bike, carried me on his shoulders, and fixed everything in the house now needs help with the car park ticket. We had lunch afterwards, a cheese sandwich and tea, and he told me stories I'd never heard. I'm cherishing every one.

Planning a big family reunion in Lagos for next December. About 60 cousins, aunties and uncles, from Houston, London, Toronto and Abuja. I've been tasked with the playlist, which means I will absolutely be in trouble no matter what I choose. Everyone's already arguing about who cooks the jollof. Bring on the noise. Bring on the dancing. See you there! 🇳🇬

My seven-year-old has discovered the word "sequel" and applies it to everything. Today he said, "Mum, today's breakfast is the sequel to yesterday's breakfast." Then, "Is the weekend the sequel to the week?" He's got a point. We spent 20 minutes discussing it over cornflakes. These are the conversations I'll miss when he's older.

Remember when your parents said "money doesn't grow on trees"? I'm now saying that to my kids and hearing my mother's voice, with her intonation. I can't believe this is what I've become. Also my father's laugh. Also my grandfather's cough. DNA is wild, and parenthood reveals you're a composite of everyone who raised you.

The town council has voted to turn the old library car park into a pocket park, with trees, benches, and a small playground. Construction starts in the spring, and local volunteers will help plant the first saplings. It's a small win, but I've been to enough meetings to know small wins don't come easily. Thanks to everyone who showed up, wrote letters and signed petitions. #localgovernment

If you're in the area this weekend: the annual village show returns on Saturday with a dog show, a vegetable contest, a tug of war and live music. Entry's £3, kids free. Last year a giant marrow won first prize, and it was 22kg. We expect a rival. The whole thing is run by volunteers, so please be nice to the people with clipboards. Hope to see you there! https://example.com/village-show

Fantastic local news: our little town now has a community theatre group that put on a one-night-only reading at the church hall. Forty chairs, fifty people, one overworked kettle. They did a medley of local history stories from the 1920s to the 1980s, and a local dairy farmer gave a surprisingly moving monologue. Lots of laughs, a few tears.

The council wants to close the swimming pool to save £400k a year. Our local swimming club has 200 kids, our parents' aqua-aerobics group has 80 members, and there's a rehab class for people recovering from surgery. Closing it would cost far more in health outcomes than it saves. Please sign the petition and email your councillor. Link in my bio. #SaveOurPool

Our local fish and chip shop, Mario's, is celebrating 50 years. He's still there every night, frying at 5pm, joking with the regulars, and running the till himself. Half the town has eaten there since they were children. On Saturday, he's giving away free chips to anyone born the year he opened. I'm a '75 baby, so I'll be first in line.

Planning permission has been submitted for a new housing estate in the field behind our school. 200 homes, a new access road, and no extra school places. I've read the application. The road assessment ignores the existing school-run traffic. I'm not a nimby, we need homes, but this needs a proper plan. Objections close on the 14th. Please write in. #planning

At 6am today, I watched two council workers fix a streetlight on my road in the pouring rain. No one else was around. They didn't complain, they just did it and left. We take a lot for granted. So thank you, whoever you were. I made a flask of tea and left it on their van, and it was gone when I came back. Good people exist.

Last week I sat on a log in an ancient Scots pine forest and counted the sounds: wind, a woodpecker, a stream, a squirrel scolding me, distant sheep, and my own breathing. Nothing else. No traffic, no alerts. The forest is a lesson in how little we need to feel awake. I left feeling rinsed clean, and I plan to go back every month. #forestbathing

Joined a beach clean-up near Lagos on Saturday with about 200 volunteers. In three hours we filled 600 bags with plastic bottles, flip-flops, fishing nets, and one broken fridge. A local school sent forty kids who did the best work of anyone. The waste problem isn't theirs, but they cleaned it up anyway. If you can, join your nearest group. #BeachCleanup

The monarch butterfly migration is one of the most extraordinary events in the natural world. Millions of tiny insects fly up to 4,000 km from Canada to central Mexico, using the sun as a compass. No single butterfly makes the whole round trip, so it takes several generations. How do the great-grandchildren know the way? We still don't fully understand. It's magic, and it's real.

Our local rewilding project has just released a pair of beavers into the river. Within a month, they'd built a small dam, which created a pool, which brought in dragonflies, frogs and a heron. Ecologists call beavers "ecosystem engineers", and now I see why. It's cheaper than any flood-defence scheme, and kinder. Come and see them at dusk. Bring a quiet voice and binoculars.

Mount Everest has been climbed more than 6,000 times, but the real story is the rubbish. Over 100 tonnes of waste, plus bodies, still sit on the mountain. Nepal now requires climbers to bring back at least 8 kg of garbage. A group of Sherpas has been carrying bags down for weeks. Hats off to them. Everest isn't a trophy, it's a place that deserves care.

There's an owl nesting in the old oak at the bottom of our garden and we've named her Hilda. Every evening around 9pm she sits on a branch and looks at us like a very serious landlord. The kids bring blankets and watch. She hasn't flinched once. It's the best entertainment in the house. No streaming needed.

Rainforests absorb about 15% of the world's annual CO2 emissions, according to the latest estimates, but deforestation continues. Brazil's rate fell sharply in 2023 and 2024, which is encouraging, while Indonesia's palm oil expansion remains a worry. It's easy to feel hopeless, but progress happens where politics, money and local communities pull in the same direction. Share stories of what works.

Okay, rant time. Spent my entire Saturday trying to get my Windows 11 laptop to sleep properly. Disabled fast startup, rolled back the chipset driver, updated the BIOS, reset the power plan, ran three different troubleshooters. Nothing worked.
Turns out a USB dongle from a keyboard I haven't used in a year was waking it up every ten minutes. A DONGLE. Microsoft really needs to show which device woke the machine in plain English instead of making us run powercfg commands like it's 1998.
Anyway, if your laptop is draining overnight, check powercfg /lastwake first. Saved you a Saturday. #Windows11 #tech
